what: Which Codex account really pays for a model request, before and after a real switch, measured on the wire.
machine: Hyper-V test machine switcher-test, Windows 11 Pro 25H2 build 26200; Hermes v0.21.5+3840.g9a0a162 (upstream 9a0a1625) installed by a normal signed-in user with the official source script
plugin: codex-account-switch 1.2.0-rc.3 development build, as installed for the 2026-09-28 real-switch receipt
method: Hermes's own command (hermes chat --oneshot --provider openai-codex -m gpt-6-astra) was pointed at a relay on the test machine's loopback using Hermes's own HERMES_CODEX_BASE_URL override. The relay read the email inside the bearer token of every request, compared the ChatGPT-Account-Id header with the token, passed the request to chatgpt.com/backend-api/codex unchanged and returned OpenAI's answer. OpenAI bills the account the token belongs to. No token or account id was printed or stored. Script: test-vm/vm-billing-proof.py.
answered_by_these_runs: A model request made after a switch is sent with the newly selected account's login, and OpenAI accepts it.
The stored order and the account on the wire agree in both directions.
not_answered_by_these_runs: A request made by a chat inside Hermes Desktop (these were Hermes's command-line one-shot requests, which read the same stored logins).
OpenAI's own usage meter moving: it reports whole percentages and one small request does not move it.
Behavior when the selected login is dead and Hermes falls through to the next one.
notes: Eleven of the fourteen requests in each run are Hermes probing a custom address for local-server features; OpenAI answers them 403 or 400. They exist only because the relay address is not the default one.
Hermes keeps a per-login request counter in memory only; it stayed 0 on disk after a successful request, so it cannot be used as evidence.
